claim: Of >100,000 patient records, ~10% of adults visited the clinic because of reduced hearing, only to learn that their hearing was clinically normal and should not cause communication difficulties.
source: Of >100,000 patient records,~10% of adults visited our clinic because of reduced hearing, only to learn that their hearing was clinically normal and should not cause communication difficulties.
evidence: Based on analysis of patient records from the Massachusetts Eye and Ear audiology database

claim: Multi-talker speech intelligibility thresholds varied widely in normal hearing adults.
source: We found that multi-talker speech intelligibility thresholds varied widely in normal hearing adults
evidence: Supported by behavioral testing data showing speech reception thresholds varying across a 0-7 dB SNR range

claim: Multi-talker speech intelligibility thresholds could be predicted from neural phase-locking to frequency modulation (FM) cues measured with ear canal EEG recordings.
source: We found that multi-talker speech intelligibility thresholds varied widely in normal hearing adults, but could be predicted from neural phase-locking to frequency modulation (FM) cues measured with ear canal EEG recordings.
evidence: Supported by correlation data between FMFR measurements and speech intelligibility thresholds

claim: Combining neural temporal fine structure processing, pupil-indexed listening effort, and behavioral FM thresholds accounted for 78% of the variability in multi-talker speech intelligibility.
source: Combining neural temporal fine structure processing, pupil-indexed listening effort, and behavioral FM thresholds accounted for 78% of the variability in multi-talker speech intelligibility.
evidence: Supported by multivariate regression analysis showing adjusted R² of 0.78

claim: Slow fluctuations in the sound pressure envelope are sufficient for accurate speech perception in quiet backgrounds.
source: Slow fluctuations in the sound pressure envelope are sufficient for accurate speech perception in quiet backgrounds (Shannon et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shannon et al., 1995

claim: Envelope cues are less useful when speech is embedded in fluctuant backgrounds comprised of multiple talkers, environmental noise or reverberation.
source: Envelope cues are less useful when speech is embedded in fluctuant backgrounds comprised of multiple talkers, environmental noise or reverberation (Zeng et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zeng et al., 2005

claim: Segregating a target speech stream from background noise requires accurate encoding of low-frequency spectral and binaural cues contained in the stimulus temporal fine structure (sTFS).
source: Under these conditions, segregating a target speech stream from background noise requires accurate encoding of low-frequency spectral and binaural cues contained in the stimulus temporal fine structure (sTFS) (Hopkins and Moore, 2009; Lorenzi et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hopkins and Moore, 2009 and Lorenzi et al., 2006

claim: Monaural sTFS cues convey acoustic signatures of target speaker identity based on the arrangement of peaks in the sound spectrum (e.g., formant frequencies of target speech).
source: Monaural sTFS cues convey acoustic signatures of target speaker identity based on the arrangement of peaks in the sound spectrum (e.g., formant frequencies of target speech)
evidence: Based on established understanding of auditory processing

claim: Binaural sTFS cues can support spatial separation of target and competing speakers via interaural phase differences.
source: while binaural sTFS cues can support spatial separation of target and competing speakers via interaural phase differences (Moore, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moore, 2014

claim: With aging and hearing loss, monaural and binaural sTFS cues become less perceptually available, even when audibility thresholds for low-frequency signals that convey sTFS cues are normal.
source: With aging and hearing loss, monaural and binaural sTFS cues become less perceptually available, even when audibility thresholds for low-frequency signals that convey sTFS cues are normal (Buss et al., 2004; DiNino et al., 2019; Füllgrabe et al., 2014; Léger et al., 2012; Lorenzi et al., 2009; Mehraei et al., 2014; Moore, 2014; Strelcyk and Dau, 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: The biological underpinnings for poor sTFS processing with aging or hearing impairment may reflect the loss of auditory nerve afferent fibers.
source: The biological underpinnings for poor sTFS processing with aging or hearing impairment are unknown, but may reflect the loss of auditory nerve afferent fibers
evidence: Presented as a hypothesis based on inference from known biology

claim: Auditory nerve afferent fibers degenerate at the rate of approximately 1000 per decade, such that only half survive by the time a typical adult has reached 40 years of age.
source: which degenerate at the rate of approximately 1000 per decade, such that only half survive by the time a typical adult has reached 40 years of age (Makary et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Makary et al., 2011 and Wu et al., 2019

claim: A selective loss of cochlear afferent fibers would not likely affect audibility thresholds, but could adversely affect the ability of the auditory system to fully exploit suprathreshold monaural and binaural sTFS cues that are critical for multi-talker speech intelligibility.
source: A selective loss of cochlear afferent fibers would not likely affect audibility thresholds, but could adversely affect the ability of the auditory system to fully exploit suprathreshold monaural and binaural sTFS cues that are critical for multi-talker speech intelligibility (Deroche et al., 2014; Hopkins et al., 2008; Jin and Nelson, 2010; Lopez-Poveda and Barrios, 2013; Moore and Glasberg, 1987; Qin and Oxenham, 2003, for review see - Moore, 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and review by Moore, 2014

claim: Accurate processing of a target speaker in a multi-talker background reflects a harmony between high-fidelity encoding of bottom-up acoustic features such as sTFS alongside cognitive signatures of active listening including attention, listening effort, memory, multisensory integration and prediction.
source: Accurate processing of a target speaker in a multi-talker background reflects a harmony between high-fidelity encoding of bottom-up acoustic features such as sTFS alongside cognitive signatures of active listening including attention, listening effort, memory, multisensory integration and prediction (Best et al., 2009; Gordon-Salant and Cole, 2016; Narayan et al., 2007; Pichora-Fuller et al., 2016; Wild et al., 2012; Winn et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Top-down assets can be leveraged to compensate for poorly resolved bottom-up sensory cues.
source: These top-down assets can be leveraged to compensate for poorly resolved bottom-up sensory cues
evidence: Based on established understanding of auditory processing and cognitive compensation

claim: Listeners with clinically normal hearing that struggle to process speech in noise might be identified by an over-reliance on top-down active listening mechanisms to de-noise a corrupted afferent speech input.
source: suggesting that listeners with clinically normal hearing that struggle to process speech in noise might be identified by an over-reliance on top-down active listening mechanisms to de-noise a corrupted afferent speech input (Besser et al., 2015; Ohlenforst et al., 2017; Winn et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Besser et al., 2015; Ohlenforst et al., 2017; Winn et al., 2015

claim: Of the 106,787 patient records that met the inclusion criteria, approximately one out of every five patients had no clinical evidence of hearing loss, defined as thresholds > 20 dB HL at test frequencies up to 8 KHz (19,952, 19%).
source: Of the 106,787 patient records that met these criteria, we found that approximately one out of every five patients had no clinical evidence of hearing loss, defined as thresholds > 20 dB HL at test frequencies up to 8 KHz (19,952, 19%, Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of patient database records shown in Figure 1B

claim: The majority of patients with normal audiograms were between 20–50 years old.
source: The majority of these individuals were between 20–50 years old (Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by age distribution data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Patients with normal audiograms had no conductive hearing impairment, nor focal threshold shifts or 'notches' in their audiograms greater than 10 dB.
source: and had no conductive hearing impairment, nor focal threshold shifts or 'notches' in their audiograms greater than 10 dB (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by audiometric analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: The thresholds between left and right ears were symmetrical within 10 dB for >95% of patients with normal audiograms.
source: The thresholds between their left and right ears were also symmetrical within 10 dB for >95% of these patients (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by between-ear threshold comparison data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: 45% of patients with normal audiograms primarily complained of decreased hearing or hearing loss.
source: Despite their clean bill of hearing health, 45% of these individuals primarily complained of decreased hearing or hearing loss (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by patient complaint data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Patients with normal audiograms are typically informed that their hearing is 'normal' and that they are not expected to experience communication problems.
source: Absent any objective measure of hearing difficulty, these patients are typically informed that their hearing is 'normal' and that they are not expected to experience communication problems.
evidence: Based on description of clinical practice

claim: 23 young or middle-aged listeners (mean age: 28.3 ± 0.9 years) matched the clinically normal hearing profile from the database.
source: To better understand the nature of their suprathreshold hearing problems, we recruited 23 young or middle-aged listeners (mean age: 28.3 ± 0.9 years) that matched the clinically normal hearing from the database profile (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by participant demographic data and audiograms shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Many subjects with clinically normal audiograms reported difficulties with speech intelligibility, particularly in listening conditions with multiple overlapping speakers.
source: Like the patients from the clinical database, the audiograms from these subjects were clinically normal, yet many reported difficulties with speech intelligibility, particularly in listening conditions with multiple overlapping speakers (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by questionnaire data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A

claim: Performance on the digits task decreased as a function of SNR.
source: Performance on the digits task decreased as a function of SNR (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by behavioral performance data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Speech reception thresholds varied widely across a 0–7 dB SNR range with a mean of 2.42 dB.
source: Speech reception thresholds, defined as the 70.7% correct point on the response curve, varied widely across a 0–7 dB SNR range with a mean of 2.42 dB (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by speech reception threshold data shown in Figure 1G

claim: Speech intelligibility thresholds were significantly correlated with subjects' self-reported difficulties in multi-speaker conditions (r = 0.46, p=0.02).
source: We found that speech intelligibility thresholds were significantly correlated with the subjects' self-reported difficulties in multi-speaker conditions, suggesting that the digits comprehension task captures aspects of their real-world communication difficulties (r = 0.46, p=0.02, Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B

claim: Subjects exhibited substantial variability in their extended high frequency thresholds (>8 kHz) despite having clinically normal audibility at lower frequencies.
source: Subjects exhibited substantial variability in their extended high frequency thresholds (>8 kHz) despite having clinically normal audibility at lower frequencies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by extended high frequency audiometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: ABR wave one amplitude and extended high frequency thresholds both showed substantial variability in subjects with clinically normal audiograms, but neither could account for performance on the competing digits task.
source: ABR wave one amplitude and extended high frequency thresholds both showed substantial variability in subjects with clinically normal audiograms, but neither could account for performance on the competing digits task (r = 0.10 p=0.64, Figure 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D

claim: Poor processing of sTFS cues has long been associated with elevated speech recognition thresholds, especially in patients with hearing loss.
source: Poor processing of sTFS cues has long been associated with elevated speech recognition thresholds, especially in patients with hearing loss (Lorenzi et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lorenzi et al., 2006

claim: FM detection thresholds varied widely between subjects.
source: FM detection thresholds varied widely between subjects (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by FM detection threshold data shown in Figure 2B

claim: FM detection thresholds were strongly correlated with performance on the competing digits task (r = 0.85, p<0.001).
source: and were strongly correlated with performance on the competing digits task (r = 0.85, p<0.001, Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: The FMFR magnitude increased as a function of FM deviation up to ~8 Hz.
source: The magnitude of the FM following response (FMFR) was computed using a heterodyne. (E) The FMFR magnitude increased as a function of FM deviation up to ~8 Hz.
evidence: Supported by FMFR growth function data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The neurophysiological FMFR was strongly predictive of FM detection thresholds determined with the psychophysical task (r = 0.66 p=0.001).
source: We found that robust low-level encoding of FM cues was highly predictive of an individual's performance on the FM psychophysical detection task (r = 0.66 p=0.001; Figure 2H)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2H

claim: The FMFR was significantly correlated with thresholds on the competing digits task (r = 0.49, p=0.02).
source: Importantly, the FMFR was also significantly correlated with thresholds on the competing digits task (r = 0.49, p=0.02, Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2I

claim: Cortical evoked potentials recorded simultaneously from the same stimuli were not correlated with either FM detection performance or speech recognition thresholds.
source: Whereas phase-locking to the sTFS cues in the FM tone was related to psychophysical performance and speech recognition thresholds, the cortical evoked potentials recorded simultaneously from the same stimuli were not correlated with either measure (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The strong association between psychophysical tests for FM detection and speech-in-noise intelligibility can be attributed, at least in part, to encoding of FM cues at early stages of auditory processing.
source: These data suggest that the strong association between psychophysical tests for FM detection and speech-in-noise intelligibility can be attributed, at least in part, to encoding of FM cues at early stages of auditory processing.
evidence: Based on inference from the correlation between FMFR and both FM detection and speech intelligibility

claim: IPD thresholds varied between 5 and 25 degrees across individual subjects.
source: IPD thresholds were variable, ranging between 5 and 25 degrees (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by IPD threshold data shown in Figure 3B

claim: There was a strong association between an individual's psychophysical threshold for IPD and the growth of the electrophysiological IPDFR (r = −0.65 p=0.001).
source: Like the FMFR above, we noted a strong association between an individual's psychophysical threshold for IPD and the growth of the electrophysiological IPDFR (r = −0.65 p=0.001, Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3F

claim: Neither the IPD psychophysical threshold, nor the IPDFR amplitude had statistically significant correlations with the digits in noise threshold.
source: More to the point, neither the IPD psychophysical threshold, nor the IPDFR amplitude had statistically significant correlations with the digits in noise threshold, confirming that task performance was specifically linked to encoding of task-relevant FM cues and not a general sensitivity to unrelated sTFS cues (IPD threshold and speech, r = 0.21 p=0.34; IPDFR and speech, r = 0.20 p=0.38, Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 3G

claim: Under isoluminous conditions, pupil diameter can provide an objective index of the sensory and cognitive challenge of processing a target speech stream in the presence of distracting speakers.
source: Under isoluminous conditions, pupil diameter can provide an objective index of the sensory and cognitive challenge of processing a target speech stream in the presence of distracting speakers (Koelewijn et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018; Winn et al., 2015; Zekveld et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on pupillometry

claim: Increased pupil dilation in low SNR listening conditions can reflect greater utilization of top-down cognitive resources to enhance attended targets.
source: Prior work has shown that increased pupil dilation in low SNR listening conditions can reflect greater utilization of top-down cognitive resources to enhance attended targets, whereas smaller pupil changes have been associated with higher fidelity bottom-up inputs that do not demand additional listening effort to process accurately (Koelewijn et al., 2012; Zekveld et al., 2014; Zekveld and Kramer, 2014) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on pupillometry and cognitive effort

claim: The fractional change in pupil diameter was linearly related to the SNR of the target speaker.
source: We confirmed here that the fractional change in pupil diameter was linearly related to the SNR of the target speaker (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by pupillometry data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Individuals with steeper pupil recruitment functions had more difficulty in the multi-talker speech task, leading to a significant correlation between min-max/halfmax pupil change and speech intelligibility threshold (r = 0.53, p=0.03).
source: We confirmed that individuals with steeper pupil recruitment functions had more difficulty in the multi-talker speech task, leading to a significant correlation between min-max/halfmax pupil change and speech intelligibility threshold (r = 0.53, p=0.03, Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: None of the neural indices (ABR wave one amplitude, FMFR, IPDFR, and pupil change) were correlated with each other.
source: Importantly, none of these indices were correlated with each other, suggesting that – in principle – each of these markers could account for statistically independent components of the total variance in speech performance (Figure 5A, right).
evidence: Supported by correlation matrix shown in Figure 5A

claim: Only FMFR and pupil showed a significant independent correlation with speech intelligibility threshold.
source: In practice, only FMFR and pupil showed a significant independent correlation with speech intelligibility threshold (Figure 5A, left).
evidence: Supported by correlation matrix shown in Figure 5A

claim: Listening effort indexed by pupil diameter explained 24% of the variance in the digit comprehension task.
source: With this model, listening effort indexed by pupil diameter explained 24% of the variance in the digit comprehension task.
evidence: Supported by multivariate regression analysis

claim: Adding monaural sTFS processing measured using the FMFR to pupil diameter increased the adjusted R2 to 49% of the overall variance.
source: Adding in monaural sTFS processing measured using the FMFR increased the adjusted R2, explaining 49% of the overall variance.
evidence: Supported by multivariate regression analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: Adding the ABR wave one to the model with pupil and FMFR provided only a minimal additional increase in predictive power, raising the total explained variance to 52%.
source: Adding in the ABR wave one provided only a minimal additional increase in predictive power, raising the total explained variance to 52% (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by multivariate regression analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: Adding additional neural markers such as the IPDFR or extended high frequency thresholds did not provide any further increase in the overall variance explained.
source: Adding additional neural markers such as the IPDFR or extended high frequency thresholds did not provide any further increase in the overall variance explained.
evidence: Supported by multivariate regression analysis

claim: The best linear model for speech intelligibility included a measure of bottom-up monaural fine structure processing and a measure of top-down listening effort.
source: Among the neural measures studied here, the best linear model for speech intelligibility included a measure of bottom-up monaural fine structure processing and a measure of top-down listening effort.
evidence: Based on multivariate regression analysis results

claim: Constructing a model with the psychophysical FM threshold along with FMFR and pupil diameter increased the variance explained to 78%.
source: Finally, even though the behavioral FM detection thresholds and the FMFR were correlated (Figure 2H), constructing a model with the psychophysical threshold along with FMFR and pupil diameter increased the variance explained to 78% (Figure 5B, gray)
evidence: Supported by multivariate regression analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: The behavioral FM detection task reflects additional aspects of auditory processing that is not captured by the combination of peripheral sTFS encoding and non-sensory measures of listening effort.
source: suggesting that the behavioral FM detection task reflects additional aspects of auditory processing that is not captured by the combination of peripheral sTFS encoding and non-sensory measures of listening effort.
evidence: Based on inference from the improved model fit when adding behavioral FM thresholds

claim: The cochlea acts as a limited-resolution filter bank that breaks down the broadband speech waveform into a spatially organized array of narrowband signals.
source: The cochlea acts as a limited-resolution filter bank that breaks down the broadband speech waveform into a spatially organized array of narrowband signals.
evidence: Based on established understanding of cochlear function

claim: STFS cues consist of rapid oscillations near the center of each cochlear filter that are encoded by phase-locked auditory nerve action potentials.
source: STFS cues consist of rapid oscillations near the center of each cochlear filter that are encoded by phase-locked auditory nerve action potentials (Henry and Heinz, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Henry and Heinz, 2013

claim: Envelope cues reflect slower changes in amplitude over time that can be encoded by the short-term firing rate statistics of auditory nerve fibers.
source: Envelope cues, by comparison, reflect slower changes in amplitude over time that can be encoded by the short-term firing rate statistics of auditory nerve fibers (Joris and Yin, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Joris and Yin, 1992

claim: The ability to detect slow rates of FM (<~6 Hz) at low carrier frequencies (<~1500 Hz) has long been associated with sTFS processing.
source: The ability to detect slow rates of FM (<~6 Hz) at low carrier frequencies (<~1500 Hz) has long been associated with sTFS processing (Moore and Sek, 1995; Paraouty et al., 2018; Sek and Moore, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Under low FM rate and low carrier frequency stimulus conditions, changes in FM are hypothesized to be conveyed by spike timing information within a cochlear filter.
source: Under these stimulus conditions, changes in FM are hypothesized to be conveyed by spike timing information within a cochlear filter (Moore and Sek, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moore and Sek, 1995

claim: The strong correlation between psychophysical thresholds for detecting pure tone FM and multi-talker speech recognition thresholds (r = 0.85) has been documented by several independent groups using a variety of speech-on-speech masking paradigms, but not with non-speech maskers.
source: The strong correlation between psychophysical thresholds for detecting pure tone FM and multi-talker speech recognition thresholds is striking (r = 0.85, Figure 2C) and has now been documented by several independent groups using a variety of speech-on-speech masking paradigms, but not with non-speech maskers (Johannesen et al., 2016; Lopez-Poveda et al., 2017; Strelcyk and Dau, 2009; Whitton et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple independent studies

claim: Some studies suggest that FM cues are converted to amplitude modulation cues at early stages of auditory processing, and hence that the perception of FM relies more on neural envelope cues.
source: The exact mechanism of FM coding by the auditory pathway is not entirely clear, with some studies suggesting that FM cues are converted to amplitude modulation cues at early stages of auditory processing, and hence that the perception of FM relies more on neural envelope cues (Ghitza, 2001; Whiteford et al., 2017; Whiteford and Oxenham, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to studies proposing envelope-based FM coding

claim: Other studies emphasize neural phase-locking to sTFS cues for FM perception.
source: while other studies emphasize neural phase-locking to sTFS cues (Moore et al., 2019; Paraouty et al., 2016; Wallaert et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies proposing phase-locking-based FM coding

claim: Many forms of cochlear dysfunction could give rise to poor sTFS processing.
source: Many forms of cochlear dysfunction could give rise to poor sTFS processing (Henry et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Henry et al., 2019

claim: When audibility thresholds are normal, the most likely explanation for poor sTFS processing involves a loss of cochlear afferent synapses onto inner hair cells.
source: though when audibility thresholds are normal, the most likely explanation involves a loss of cochlear afferent synapses onto inner hair cells.
evidence: Based on inference from known mechanisms of hearing dysfunction

claim: Auditory nerve fiber loss has been observed in cochlear regions with normal thresholds in many animal species as well as post-mortem analysis of human temporal bone specimens.
source: Auditory nerve fiber loss has been observed in cochlear regions with normal thresholds in many animal species as well as post-mortem analysis of human temporal bone specimens (Furman et al., 2013; Gleich et al., 2016; Kujawa and Liberman, 2009; Möhrle et al., 2016; Valero et al., 2017; Viana et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies in animals and humans

claim: In humans, appreciable auditory nerve fiber loss begins in early adulthood, well before degeneration is noted in cochlear sensory cells or spiral ganglion cell bodies.
source: In humans, recent findings suggest that appreciable auditory nerve fiber loss begins in early adulthood, well before degeneration is noted in cochlear sensory cells or spiral ganglion cell bodies (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2019

claim: In animal models, a loss of cochlear afferent synapses disrupts temporal coding of amplitude modulation on a variety of time scales without permanently elevating pure tone thresholds.
source: In animal models, a loss of cochlear afferent synapses disrupts temporal coding of amplitude modulation on a variety of time scales without permanently elevating pure tone thresholds, consistent with observations made in our subject cohort (Bakay et al., 2018; Parthasarathy and Kujawa, 2018; Shaheen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to animal model studies

claim: In humans, it is impossible to directly assess the status of cochlear afferent synapses in vivo.
source: In humans, it is impossible to directly assess the status of cochlear afferent synapses in vivo
evidence: Based on current technical limitations

claim: Indirect proxies for cochlear afferent innervation may be possible.
source: though indirect proxies for cochlear afferent innervation may be possible (for recent reviews see - Bharadwaj et al., 2019; Bramhall et al., 2019; Guest et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent review articles

claim: Speech perception does not arise directly from the auditory nerve, but rather reflects the patterning of neural activity in the central auditory pathway.
source: Speech perception does not arise directly from the auditory nerve, but rather reflects the patterning of neural activity in the central auditory pathway.
evidence: Based on established understanding of auditory processing

claim: Hearing loss profoundly affects gene expression, cellular morphology, neurotransmitter levels and physiological signal processing at every stage of the central pathway - from cochlear nucleus to cortex.
source: Hearing loss profoundly affects gene expression, cellular morphology, neurotransmitter levels and physiological signal processing at every stage of the central pathway - from cochlear nucleus to cortex - and these central sequelae resulting from a peripheral insult would also be expected to affect the neural representation of speech in ways that cannot be accounted for purely by peripheral measures (Auerbach et al., 2019; Balaram et al., 2019; Caspary et al., 2008; Chambers et al., 2016; Möhrle et al., 2016; Parthasarathy et al., 2019; Sarro et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on central auditory plasticity

claim: The psychophysical FM detection threshold was more highly correlated with speech recognition than the neural measure of low-level FM encoding.
source: To this point, the psychophysical FM detection threshold was more highly correlated with speech recognition than the neural measure of low-level FM encoding, suggesting that the behavioral task captured additional aspects of FM detection not present in the FMFR.
evidence: Based on comparison of correlation coefficients between behavioral and neural measures with speech performance

claim: In a recent placebo-controlled auditory training study, thresholds could improve by ~1.5 dB SNR on the digits task without any improvement in FM detection threshold, or any other marker of bottom-up processing.
source: In a recent placebo-controlled auditory training study, we observed that thresholds could improve by ~1.5 dB SNR on the same digits task used here without any improvement in FM detection threshold, or any other marker of bottom-up processing, again pointing towards the critical involvement of top-down active listening mechanisms in multi-talker speech perception (Whitton et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Whitton et al., 2017

claim: Adding neural markers of higher-order stream segregation to the multivariate model would very likely capture even more of the unexplained variability in multi-talker speech intelligibility.
source: Adding neural markers of higher-order stream segregation to the multivariate model (Divenyi, 2014; Krishnan et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2017; Shamma et al., 2011; Teki et al., 2013) or direct neural speech decoding (Ding and Simon, 2012; Ding and Simon, 2009; Maddox and Lee, 2018; Mesgarani et al., 2014; Mesgarani et al., 2008; Pasley et al., 2012; Presacco et al., 2016) would very likely capture even more of the unexplained variability in multi-talker speech intelligibility
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citations to relevant research areas

claim: Neural markers of higher-order stream segregation offer less insight into the particular mode of sensory failure than FMFR and are considerably harder to implement in a clinical setting.
source: though they offer less insight into the particular mode of sensory failure than FMFR and are also considerably harder to implement in a clinical setting.
evidence: Based on inference about clinical applicability

claim: Individuals who struggle most to follow conversations in noisy, social settings might be identified both by poor bottom-up processing of rapid temporal cues in speech and also by an over-utilization of top-down active listening resources.
source: Our findings suggest that the individuals who struggle most to follow conversations in noisy, social settings might be identified both by poor bottom-up processing of rapid temporal cues in speech and also by an over-utilization of top-down active listening resources.
evidence: Based on inference from the study findings

claim: The interplay between bottom-up and top-down processing is likely more complex than a simple tradeoff where poor sTFS processing is linked to strong pupil-indexed listening effort, or vice versa.
source: The interplay between bottom-up and top-down processing is likely more complex than a simple tradeoff where poor sTFS processing is linked to strong pupil-indexed listening effort, or vice versa, as we observed no linear correlation between these variables and no pattern emerged on a subject by subject basis (Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on inference from lack of correlation between FMFR and pupil measures shown in Figure 5A

claim: Patients with bilateral normal audiograms represented ~19% of the patient population at the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary.
source: Patients with bilateral normal audiograms represented ~19% of the patient population at the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary
evidence: Based on database analysis

claim: The combination of an increased lifespan and the increased use of in-ear listening devices will likely exacerbate the societal impact of hidden hearing disorder.
source: The combination of an increased lifespan and the increased use of in-ear listening devices will likely exacerbate the societal impact of hidden hearing disorder
evidence: Based on speculation about future trends

claim: Hidden hearing disorder will leave hundreds of millions of people straining to follow conversations in noisy, reverberant environments typically encountered in the workplace and social settings.
source: leaving hundreds of millions of people straining to follow conversations in noisy, reverberant environments typically encountered in the workplace and social settings (Goman and Lin, 2016; Hind et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2011; Ruggles et al., 2012; Ruggles et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on hearing difficulties

claim: The standard of care at hearing health clinics include measures of pure tone thresholds, otoacoustic emissions, middle ear reflexes and recognition of individual words presented in silence.
source: The standard of care at hearing health clinics include measures of pure tone thresholds, otoacoustic emissions, middle ear reflexes and recognition of individual words presented in silence.
evidence: Based on knowledge of current clinical practice

claim: Standard clinical tests are useful in diagnosing late-stage hearing loss commonly found with aging, or exposure to ototoxic drugs or intense noise, where there is pathology in the sound transduction machinery of the middle and inner ear.
source: These tests are useful in diagnosing late-stage hearing loss commonly found with aging, or exposure to ototoxic drugs or intense noise, where there is pathology in the sound transduction machinery of the middle and inner ear.
evidence: Based on knowledge of clinical test utility

claim: New diagnostic measures and interventions are needed for individuals who struggle to follow conversations in noisy, social environments and avoid seeking clinical care for their hearing difficulties.
source: New diagnostic measures and interventions are needed for the silent majority, who struggle to follow conversations in noisy, social environments and avoid seeking clinical care for their hearing difficulties.
evidence: Based on inference from the study findings and clinical need

claim: A simple battery of behavioral and physiological tests can account for nearly 80% of the variability in a test of multi-talker speech intelligibility that does not involve linguistic cues.
source: Here, we present a simple battery of behavioral and physiological tests that can account for nearly 80% of the variability in a test of multi-talker speech intelligibility that does not involve linguistic cues.
evidence: Based on the multivariate regression analysis results

claim: Low-channel EEG systems and pupillometry cameras are relatively low-cost and could be put to use in clinical settings to provide patients with an objective measure for their perceptual difficulties.
source: Low-channel EEG systems and pupillometry cameras are relatively low-cost and could – in theory – be put to use in clinical settings to provide patients with an objective measure for their perceptual difficulties and provide hearing health providers with an objective readout for their therapeutic drugs or devices.
evidence: Based on speculation about clinical implementation
